source_witness.passage: (C) Controlled substance traffickers Any alien who the consular officer or the Attorney General knows or has reason to believe— (i) is or has been an illicit trafficker in any controlled substance or in any listed chemical (as defined in section 802 of title 21), or is or has been a knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator, or colluder with others in the illicit trafficking in any such controlled or listed substance or chemical, or endeavored to do so; or (ii) is the spouse, son, or daughter of an alien inadmissible under clause (i), has, within the previous 5 years, obtained any financial or other benefit from the illicit activity of that alien, and knew or reasonably should have known that the financial or other benefit was the product of such illicit activity, is inadmissible.

corrections.before_meaning:
The exact amendment No.2 in Part B of House Report 119-2, offered by Trahan as Pettersen's designee, would replace the applicability paragraph with a condition on THIS ACT AND ALL AMENDMENTS MADE BY THIS ACT taking effect on the date the Secretary of Health and Human Services AND the Attorney General jointly certify IN THE FEDERAL REGISTER that this Act will lead to a reduction in overdose deaths. The condition is global, including the proposed statutory class-control predicate incorporated by the identified Immigration grounds, and is not confined to one scheduling clause. It is not certification by either official alone, an observed reduction in deaths, a mandatory certification date or a change to the existing temporary control. The amendment FAILED and the condition was not adopted. Yea supports adding this condition; Nay opposes adding it, without establishing a position on whole-bill passage or a preferred alternative. The adopted rule's Part A technical corrections and this rejected Part B condition remain distinct.
The Immigration relationship is confined to the controlled-substance classification expressly incorporated by the identified grounds, rather than every criminal-law consequence. Under existing 8 U.S.C. 1182(a), subject to the chapter's exceptions, aliens inadmissible under the listed paragraphs are ineligible for visas and admission. Section 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(II) retains conviction, admission of committing the offense, or admission of acts constituting its essential elements; a violation, conspiracy or attempt to violate a State, United States or foreign law or regulation relating to a controlled substance defined in 21 U.S.C. 802 is still required. The youth and petty-crime exceptions printed in clause (ii) apply to the moral-turpitude branch in clause (i)(I), not automatically to this controlled-substance branch. Section 1182(a)(2)(C)(i) separately requires the consular officer or Attorney General to know or have reason to believe the alien is or has been an illicit trafficker, knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator or colluder, or has endeavored to engage in the specified trafficking; it includes the separately printed listed-chemical alternative and does not substitute a conviction requirement for these tests. Clause (C)(ii) separately requires a spouse, son or daughter of an alien inadmissible under (C)(i), a financial or other benefit obtained within the previous five years from that person's illicit activity, and knowledge or reasonable grounds for knowing its illicit source. Relationship alone does not suffice.
Under 8 U.S.C. 1227(a), an alien, including an alien crewman, IN AND ADMITTED TO THE UNITED STATES is subject to removal UPON THE ORDER OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL if within a listed deportable class. Its controlled-substance conviction ground in 1227(a)(2)(B)(i) separately requires conviction at any time after admission for a violation, conspiracy or attempt to violate the identified State, United States or foreign law or regulation relating to a substance defined by 21 U.S.C. 802, except a single offense involving possession for one's own use of 30 grams or less of marijuana. Neither classification alone nor this House choice establishes an individual's deportability or produces an automatic removal order. The separate drug-abuser/addict ground in (B)(ii) is not given an express section 802 incorporation that it does not print. Existing 1182(h) allows only its separately qualified discretionary waiver, with the controlled-substance part confined to a single simple-possession offense involving 30 grams or less of marijuana and its other eligibility, exclusions and discretion preserved. Section 1182(d)(3)(A) separately permits qualified temporary nonimmigrant admission in the Attorney General's discretion, with recommendation/approval or documentation requirements and its printed exclusions and conditions; this is not an all-drug immigrant waiver or an entitlement. These grounds and waivers are not newly enacted or repealed by this proposal.
Section 802(6) defines a controlled substance through inclusion in Schedules I-V. The February 6, 2025 baseline already included temporary Schedule I class control under 21 C.F.R. 1308.11(h)(30). The original order ran February 6, 2018-February 6, 2020; Public Law 116-114 kept it in effect notwithstanding other law, and the April 2020 correction expressly preserved uninterrupted control despite the electronic-CFR omission, distinguishing effectiveness from applicability. The latest pre-vote extension in Public Law 118-158 section 5105 continued that order through March 31, 2025. H.R.27 would ADD statutory Schedule I coverage without that temporary March 31 expiry, under its own definition and exceptions. It does not say it repeals or replaces temporary paragraph (h)(30), establish first-ever class control, or make every listed substance's status irrevocable. The source-supported proposed continuation of an expressly incorporated classification is the bounded domain mechanism; no universal criminal-law or collateral-consequence domain rule is accepted.
The temporary order prints isomers, esters, ethers, salts and salts of those forms, excluding substances under another DEA Controlled Substance Code Number and those with an FDA section 505 exemption or approval. H.R.27's proposed Schedule I(e)(1) instead prints its own material/compound/mixture/preparation and salts/isomers/salts-of-isomers language, unless specifically exempted or in another schedule. Its definition uses one or more of five specified structural modifications: phenyl-portion replacement in the phenethyl group, listed substitution in/on that group, listed substitution in/on the piperidine ring, replacement of the aniline ring with an aromatic monocycle, or replacement of the N-propionyl group by another acyl group. Paragraph (e)(3) excludes substances controlled by Attorney General action under section 201 or expressly listed in another schedule; the temporary FDA phrase is not repeated verbatim. The proposed class and temporary class are not declared identical chemical sets, and no particular medicine or substance is classified here. Medical fentanyl's existing Schedule II listing remains distinct; this is not moving all fentanyl into Schedule I. Existing scheduling/removal authority and the proposal's exemptions remain. An optional Attorney General list does not determine the status of every qualifying substance; absence from that list does not negate statutory control under the proposed definition.
The global effectiveness condition would gate the proposed class coverage and the Act's other amendments, including research-registration, technical dispensing and specified penalty amendments. The amendment does not rewrite every separately printed enactment-relative deadline or establish an actual lapse in control. The separate passage vote is not this amendment choice. The existing temporary baseline, independent offense/admission/knowledge/timing/exception predicates, and individual removal-order requirement remain; no certification, enforcement result, personal legal finding, component preference, motive or enactment is inferred.
